pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): insect communication and behaviour — the bee WAGGLE DANCE (tells hive-mates the direction and distance to flowers), ant PHEROMONE trails, firefly light flashes, cricket chirps, and the monarch butterfly MIGRATION across continents. How insects 'talk' without words.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4/Y5 living things and animal behaviour contexts; working-scientifically (interpreting how signals carry information).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 4-LS1-2 (animals sense, process and respond to information) and 3-LS2-1 (group behaviour); communication as information transfer.
• Operational details — the unifying idea is that a SIGNAL carries INFORMATION: the waggle dance encodes two variables (angle to the sun = direction; duration = distance); pheromone trails are chemical messages that build up and fade; flashes are species-specific codes. The waggle dance is the star because it's a decodable, two-variable code — genuinely astonishing. Migration adds navigation over vast distance across generations. Avoid over-anthropomorphising (bees don't 'talk' with intent/words).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): names three ways insects communicate. Tier B (age 10): explains what the waggle dance conveys (direction AND distance). Tier C (age 11): explains how a signal encodes information (angle=direction, length=distance) and describes the monarch migration's remarkable distance/navigation.
bestPractices: Centre the idea that a signal carries INFORMATION — the waggle dance encodes two variables at once (direction and distance).
Let children decode AND produce signals so the code is understood from both ends.
Show pheromone trails as chemical messages that build up and fade, not permanent paths.
Avoid over-anthropomorphising — insects signal, they don't 'talk' with words or intent.
Use the monarch migration to add scale and navigation, connecting behaviour to survival.
keyRepresentations: A waggle-dance decoder linking angle→direction and duration→distance.
An ant pheromone-trail that strengthens with traffic and fades over time.
A monarch migration map across a continent.
commonMisconceptions: 'Bees talk / have a language like ours' — they signal information, without words or conscious intent.
'The waggle dance only shows direction' — it encodes distance too (via duration).
'Ant trails are permanent roads' — they are chemical signals that evaporate unless reinforced.
'All fireflies flash the same' — patterns are species-specific codes.
'One butterfly makes the whole migration round-trip' — the monarch migration spans multiple generations.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11, this topic builds the idea that insect communication is a SIGNAL carrying INFORMATION that changes another insect's behaviour, without words. The star example is the honeybee waggle dance, which encodes two variables at once: the angle of the straight 'waggle run' gives direction (on the vertical comb in the dark hive, the run's angle from straight up stands for the flowers' angle from the sun's direction), and the duration of the waggle run gives distance. Supporting examples include ant pheromone trails (chemical messages that build up with traffic and fade unless reinforced), firefly flash patterns (species-specific codes), and cricket chirps. The monarch butterfly migration adds scale and navigation across generations, and is deliberately used as a contrast — remarkable behaviour that is NOT communication. Children should both DECODE and PRODUCE signals so the code is understood from both ends. Avoid over-anthropomorphising: insects signal, they do not 'talk' with words or conscious intent.

activities.title: Decode and perform the waggle dance
feedback: When the heading matches the dance angle and the set distance matches the waggle duration: 'You landed on the flowers — you read both parts of the code.'
When the direction is right but distance is wrong: 'Right way, wrong distance — the LENGTH of each waggle run tells you how far, not just the angle.'
When the angle is misread: 'You went the wrong way — the ANGLE of the straight waggle run from straight up on the comb is the angle to fly measured from the sun's direction.'
When producing the dance: 'Check both variables — does your dance angle point toward the patch, and does your waggle length match how far it is?'
activities.rationale: Letting children decode AND produce the signal makes 'a signal carries information' concrete and reveals the two-variable structure (angle=direction, duration=distance) that a single-fact statement hides. An interactive encode/decode loop lets learners test and correct their reading; a fixed diagram can show the key but cannot provide this trial-and-correction. Efficacy of the specific interactive format is a proposal, not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
KS2 pupils study animal behaviour within living things and their habitats and interpret how information/signals function.
learnerActions: Watch a forager bee perform a waggle dance: a straight 'waggle run' tilted at an angle, then a loop back, repeated over and over.

Read the two pieces of information: use the ANGLE of the straight run from straight up on the comb to work out the direction to the flowers (that same angle measured from the sun's direction), and use how LONG each waggle run lasts to judge the distance.
Set your heading at the dance's angle measured from the sun's direction and set a distance from the waggle duration, then 'fly out' to try to reach the flower patch.
If you overshoot, fall short, or head the wrong way, watch the bee dance again and adjust your reading.
Then swap roles: given a flower patch in a chosen position, perform the correct dance (right angle, right waggle length) so hive-mates could find it.
activities.intendedInsight: The little dance is a real message that carries TWO pieces of information at once — which direction and how far — a decodable code, not just excited wiggling. Producing the dance as well as reading it shows the code works from both ends.

activities.title: Lay an ant trail that strengthens and fades
feedback: If a learner treats the trail as permanent: 'Watch again with no ants using it — the trail fades. It only stays while ants keep reinforcing it.'
If a learner says it is not communication because there are no words: 'The chemical IS the message — it changes where other ants go, so it carries information.'
activities.rationale: Showing the trail build up and fade targets the 'ant trails are permanent roads' misconception directly and broadens 'communication' to a chemical channel. A dynamic strengthen/fade behaviour makes the temporary, reinforced nature visible in a way a still picture of a path does not.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
Animals receive information through senses, process it, and respond in ways that aid survival, including in groups (4-LS1-2, 3-LS2-1).
learnerActions: Draw a scent (pheromone) trail between the nest and a food source.
Watch what happens as more ants travel the trail — notice it strengthens with traffic.
Stop the traffic and observe the trail fade over time.
Explain in your own words why a trail is NOT a permanent road and what information it carries to other ants.
activities.intendedInsight: A pheromone trail is a chemical message: it carries 'food this way', builds up when reinforced by traffic, and evaporates when not — so it is a signal, not a fixed path.

activities.title: Match firefly flash patterns to species
feedback: If a learner assumes all fireflies flash the same: 'Compare two patterns — the timing differs. The pattern is a code that usually identifies the species.'
If the pattern is reproduced incorrectly: 'Check the timing and order of the flashes — that sequence is what carries the message.'
activities.rationale: A light channel reinforces that communication is any signal that carries information, and addresses the 'all fireflies flash the same' misconception. Reproducing the pattern adds a production step rather than recognition alone. No cited source directly addresses firefly signalling, so this activity is an extrapolation from the general signal-carries-information principle.
learnerActions: Observe different firefly flash patterns (timing and sequence of flashes).
Reproduce a given species' flash pattern.
Match a flash pattern to the species that uses it, and explain who the signal is for and why (finding a mate).
activities.intendedInsight: Flashes are species-specific codes — a signal using light. Different species use different patterns, so the pattern itself carries meaning to the right receiver.

activities.title: Navigate the monarch migration — and ask: is this communication?
feedback: If a learner says one butterfly makes the whole round-trip: 'The journey spans several generations — different butterflies complete different legs.'
If a learner calls migration a form of communication: 'Ask: is one monarch sending a signal to change another's behaviour? Migration is travelling and navigating, not signalling.'
activities.rationale: Using migration as a deliberate non-example (a counterexample) prompts learners to apply the definition of communication rather than memorise a list, and adds scale/navigation connecting behaviour to survival.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
learnerActions: Trace the monarch butterfly migration across a continent-spanning map, following the route over thousands of kilometres.
Describe what makes the journey remarkable in terms of distance and navigation.
Note that the full round-trip spans multiple generations — one butterfly does not complete it alone.
Decide and justify: is migrating the same as communicating, or is it something different?
activities.intendedInsight: Migration is a remarkable navigational behaviour, but it is NOT communication — it does not pass information to another insect to change its behaviour. This contrast sharpens the definition of communication.

activities.title: Explain what the waggle dance does (diagnostic discussion)
feedback: If a learner says the bee is just excited/random: 'Move the food and the dance angle and length change with it — a meaning that reliably maps to location is information, not excitement.'

If a learner says the bee flies off and the others just follow behind: 'The other bees read the dance INSIDE the hive, then fly out on their own. The information is transmitted, not demonstrated by leading — telling where is different from guiding there.'

If a learner says insects can't communicate because they can't talk: 'Communication is any signal carrying information — chemical trails, light flashes, chirps, and the dance all change another insect's behaviour without words.'
activities.rationale: A two-tier discussion (what the dance does, then what information and why it is communication) discriminates a signal-with-meaning from a meaningless wiggle and targets the three main misconceptions directly with contrastive moves.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
KS2 pupils study animal behaviour within living things and their habitats and interpret how information/signals function.
learnerActions: Consider the claim: 'When a honeybee finds flowers, it just gets excited and wiggles about.' Decide whether that is right.
Explain what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
Answer a follow-up: HOW does one dance show BOTH direction AND distance — what part of the dance carries each?
Explain whether an ant's chemical trail and a firefly's flash also count as communication, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Communication is a signal that carries information and changes another animal's behaviour. The dance is not mere excitement: the angle encodes direction and the waggle duration encodes distance, and hive-mates decode it inside the hive before flying out on their own.

constraints: Centre the idea that a SIGNAL carries INFORMATION; keep the two-variable structure of the waggle dance (angle=direction, waggle duration=distance) explicit.
Avoid over-anthropomorphising: insects signal, they do not 'talk' with words or conscious intent. Use 'the dance carries information' rather than 'the bee says'.
Present pheromone trails as chemical messages that build up with traffic and fade unless reinforced — not permanent roads.
Treat firefly patterns as species-specific; do not imply all fireflies flash identically.
Use migration as a non-example of communication and make clear the round-trip spans multiple generations, not one individual.
A tap-to-reveal annotated scene or a static waggle-dance key can explain each method but does not provide the decode/produce loop; treat it as a scaffold, not the core activity.

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice checks can assess decoding but do not, on their own, elicit independent production of a signal; include a production step (performing the dance, reproducing a flash pattern, laying a trail).
An in-role 'forager bee' narration can introduce the dance, but learners still need to decode the two variables themselves, not just be told the answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

All three source claims are marked verified:false in the source row; confidence was legacy-labelled 'high', but the efficacy and necessity of any specific interactive format are not established by the cited sources.

The firefly flash-pattern activity is not directly supported by any cited source claim (the behaviour claim covers only bees, ants and monarchs); sourceClaims set to [] and the activity flagged as an extrapolation.

Self-audit: the von Frisch waggle-dance description (angle relative to the sun = direction; waggle-run duration = distance) is stated consistently across the source and retained as-is; no arithmetic or force/motion content required correction.

The original rationale asserted 'no static image can' convey that a signal carries information and that interactive decode 'teaches far better'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not supported by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped scaffold/affordance statements.

Activity[0]'s second sourceClaim (KS2 'interpret how information/signals function') is retained because the activity enacts interpreting a signal; it supports the interpret/decode act, not the untested efficacy of the interactive format, which remains qualified.

The monarch-as-non-example framing is pedagogically useful, but monarch navigation mechanisms are summarised at a child-appropriate level; the sources cite only migration distance, not navigation-mechanism detail.

probeDeeper: 'You said the dance tells the others where the flowers are. HOW does one dance show both the direction AND how far? What in the dance carries each part?'
'An ant lays a chemical trail instead of dancing. Is that communication too? What information does the trail carry?' (different channel, same idea)
'A firefly flashing a pattern — who is it signalling to, and what for?'
'A monarch butterfly migrates thousands of miles alone. Is migrating the same as communicating, or something different?' (counterexample: remarkable behaviour that is NOT communication)
assess.correctAnswer: It's not just excitement — the waggle dance is communication. Through the direction and length of the waggle, the bee tells its hive-mates WHERE the flowers are: the angle of the dance shows the direction (relative to the sun) and the length/duration of the waggle shows the distance. Other bees read this and fly to the food. It counts as communication because one bee is deliberately passing useful information that changes what the other bees do — even though there are no words.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the dance is just random movement or excitement, carrying no information
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the dance is systematic: change the food's location and the dance angle/length changes too. A meaning that reliably maps to location = information, not excitement.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the bee is just excited and wiggling about
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bee is excited/happy/wiggling for no reason; can't say the dance means anything

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the bee physically leads the others to the flowers rather than encoding location in the dance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out the other bees decode the dance INSIDE the hive and then fly out on their own. The information is transmitted, not demonstrated by leading. Separate 'telling where' from 'guiding there'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bee flies off and the others simply follow behind it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the bee flies out and the others just follow it; misses that the dance itself tells them where before they leave

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks insects communicate the way humans do — with sounds/words meaning things — and misses non-word channels (chemical trails, light, vibration)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden 'communication' to any signal that carries information: ant pheromone trails (chemical), firefly flashes (light), cricket chirps (sound), bee dance (movement). Each changes another insect's behaviour without words.
errorPatterns.distractor: Insects can't really communicate because they can't talk
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes communication must be 'talking'; struggles to count pheromone trails or firefly flashes as communication

responseLevels.gap: Says the dance is just excitement/random, or thinks insects can't communicate because they can't talk.
responseLevels.full: Explains the waggle dance encodes direction and distance to food, that hive-mates decode it and act on it, and defines communication as a signal carrying information — transferring to other channels (pheromone trails, flashes) AND distinguishing migration (not communication), showing the concept rather than memorised examples.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the waggle dance means something and lists other examples, but can't say what information it carries (direction + distance) or why a signal counts as communication — separate facts without the 'carries information that changes behaviour' idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, it goes back to the hive and does a 'waggle dance'. A child says: 'The bee is just excited and wiggling about.' Is that right? Tell me what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands insect communication says the signal CARRIES INFORMATION that changes another insect's behaviour — and can name what the waggle encodes (direction + distance). A child with a shallow view says the bee is just excited/random, or that it 'shows' the others by leading them, missing that the dance itself encodes direction and distance. The second tier (what information, why communication) separates a signal-with-meaning from a meaningless wiggle.
